https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-p.text: BERLIN — Europe is scrambling for more Patriot interceptors to donate to an increasingly desperate Ukraine, which is racing to reinforce its ballistic missile defenses before Russia’s expected winter assault. Kyiv is seeking hundreds of interceptors, but new production will come too late, the war with Iran has strained U.S. supplies, and several of Ukraine’s leading European backers say they have few left that they can safely donate. “Over the last few months, Russia fires more missiles a week at us than we get from partners over months," former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said last week . In July, Ukrainian air defense intercepted only 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles, with another 40 failing to reach their targets, Ukraine's defense ministry said . Advertisement Advertisement Germany, one of Ukraine’s top military aid donors, has already transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. But Berlin must now balance Kyiv’s increasingly urgent needs against the minimum stocks required to protect Germany and meet its NATO commitments. Other European countries are also weighing whether to hang on to their interceptors or give them to Ukraine. “We are really reaching our limits here,” Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, a senior German defense ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin shortly after last month’s NATO summit in Ankara. “We also have to ensure our own protection.” Berlin and other Northern European capitals have urged counterparts elsewhere on the continent to examine what more military equipment and financial support they could release. “I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO. “All the European countries have to step up.” That's putting pressure on countries with stocks of Patriot interceptors like Poland, Spain and Greece. The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles, which are among Ukraine’s few effective defenses against fast-moving Russian ballistic weapons. Ukraine can use other, often cheaper, air-defense systems against drones and cruise missiles. The country is racing to develop its homegrown Freyja interceptor, but the anti-ballistic system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can fill that role. Advertisement Advertisement Until Freyja is ready, Ukraine needs an immediate answer to Russia’s ballistic missiles. “One of the priority directions is Patriot — PAC-3 or PAC-2,” Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told POLITICO. “The first [solution] is buying, or receiving from stockpiles, PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors.” Stuck in Washington The Patriot dependence makes U.S. President Donald Trump essential to Kyiv: Most PAC-3 interceptors are produced in America, which means their sale and any production deals are subject to White House decisions. During Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's meeting with Trump last month, “The main topic was Patriot interceptors,” according to a senior official familiar with the talks. Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump speak on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 8, 2026. | Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images Trump raised hopes at the Ankara summit when he said Ukraine would be allowed to produce U.S.-designed Patriot interceptors under license — a step that could eventually reduce Kyiv’s dependence on scarce American deliveries. U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker made clear that production would not solve the immediate shortage. “A long-term production agreement will not be concluded before this winter,” he told Fox Business, and manufacturing the first missiles would take longer still. Advertisement Advertisement But Trump has now walked that back, last week saying: "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology." Following a Reuters report that the U.S. had almost exhausted its missile stocks thanks to the war against Iran, Trump is now focusing on rebuilding U.S. supplies. Asked on Thursday about Zelenskyy’s calls for more Patriot missiles, he said: “We want missiles too.” Ukraine has also signed a deal to get PAC-2 interceptors being made in Germany, but they are unlikely to arrive before next year. Faced with a shortage of interceptors, Kyiv is now looking at a more aggressive campaign to hit Russian launchers. "The Russians must understand that a few minutes after the launch, the entire team that launches the rocket must die from our ballistic missile," Fedorov said. Europe’s unbalanced effort That puts the immediate burden on Europe, where allies are once again searching their own arsenals — and one another’s — for interceptors that could reach Ukraine before winter. Advertisement Advertisement Germany supplied three Patriot systems from its own military stocks and subsequently arranged two more through a deal under which the U.S. would replenish the Bundeswehr. The Netherlands assembled the components for another complete system, including five launchers, a radar and missiles. But with stocks now stretched thin, governments face limits of their own. Warsaw confirmed in July that it had released several PAC-3 interceptors after requests from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and senior U.S. commanders. Polish outlet Defence24 reported that just five missiles were transferred. Mark Rutte speaks at a press conference ahead of a NATO summit in Ankara on July 6, 2026. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images Even that triggered a political backlash. Opposition lawmakers accused the government of weakening the country’s defenses at a time when Russian missiles and drones have repeatedly strayed across its border. Countries closer to Russia are now becoming less likely to give up existing Patriots because their armed forces already regarded their air defenses as insufficient for national requirements, according to a European diplomat granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic contacts. That is shifting attention toward Southern European countries, which have contributed less to Ukraine than Germany and many Northern European donors. Advertisement Advertisement Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez confirmed in 2024 that Madrid was sending missiles to Ukraine, but the government has not disclosed their type or amount. Spain's defense ministry did not respond to a question from POLITICO whether it had recently been approached for more interceptors or was considering another transfer. It instead pointed to Spain’s wider military support for Ukraine and its NATO commitments. Greece — which traditionally sees fellow NATO member Turkey as its greatest security threat — has not announced any Patriot transfers to Ukraine. Greek media reported in July that Ukraine had requested as many as 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Athens. The Greek defense ministry did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment. Prying open Europe’s arsenals This isn’t the first time European allies have had to cobble together Patriot missile deliveries from their own limited stocks. At a February meeting, Ukraine's Fedorov said he and Rutte worked through a list of interceptors held by European allies, asking governments for whatever they could spare. Advertisement “Dear defense minister of Poland, can you give us five?” Fedorov recalled in this week's interview. Berlin offered to top up the effort. “If you get 20 out of all the countries, I'll give you an extra five,” Fedorov quoted German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius as saying. “That’s the exercise we had to perform to get more than 20. And it is a hard mission.” Kyiv is continuing those types of talks with its allies. “Of course, Ukrainian diplomats have been working with Spain, Greece and everyone in the world who has [PACs],” said the senior official familiar with the talks. “Everything depends on the U.S., and the lack of political will to help influences everyone else.” “The American administration could have helped, but they don’t do this. And as the result it’s been hard with everyone else,” they added. For Kyiv, the arguments over allied stockpiles are unfolding against a ticking clock. With demand for PAC-3 interceptors surging in the Middle East, the Pentagon replenishing its own stock and many European countries worrying about their own ability to fend off a future Russian attack, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was struggling to buy, exchange or secure any available rounds. “We are literally fighting for every missile,” Sybiha said. Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv. Advertisement

http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/05/two-p.text: Rescuers in Nepal continue to pull people out on Saturday, 10 days after the devastating floods hit along the Nepal-Tibet border, meanwhile thousands of people are still missing.In separate situations, one Chinese man and a woman were found alive by rescue teams.The woman was found alive in her house buried under thick mud and debris in flood-hit Nuwakot, footage released by Nepal's army shows the woman covered in mud, officials say she has been airlifted to Kathmandu.In parallel, Nepal's prime minister's office posted on social media that the man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel. He is the third person to be pulled from the Trishuli hydropower project, as two Nepalese workers were rescued on Friday.The man was pulled from a 225-meter tunnel and evacuated in a helicopter by Nepalese military personnel who were working alongside South Korean disaster experts according to Nepal's army.About 900 workers are still missing and 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels across 12 hydropower projects where rescue efforts have focused, according to authorities.The devasting flash floods which hit the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun left at least 1,300 people killed, while more than 5,000 remain missing. The disaster was likely caused by a glacier collapse, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.Specialised teams from China, India, South Korea and the United States have joined search efforts in hope of finding survivors.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/05/situ.text: Russian health authorities said on Monday that a laboratory assistant at an anti-plague institute in Siberia who died last week did not have plague, even as quarantine restrictions remained in place across multiple hospitals in the region.Daria Shipilova, 28, a staff member at the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, may have contracted pneumonic plague after a test tube broke in the laboratory, regional outlets reported, citing unnamed sources close to regional security services.Authorities placed more than 60 institute employees under isolation inside the building from Friday.A relative of one employee told Siberia.Realii they slept on the floor and chairs without beds, with food parcels passed through a checkpoint. No positive test results had emerged among staff by Saturday, the relative said.Several Irkutsk hospitals were also placed under quarantine, including three city clinical hospitals, the Ivano-Matreninsky children's hospital and the city maternity hospital.The Central District Hospital in Shelekhov, a satellite town where Shipilova lived, was also closed. Sources for People of Baikal said ambulances transporting contacts of Shipilova for examination had been escorted by FSB officers since Thursday.A mask mandate was introduced at the Irkutsk Aluminium Plant in Shelekhov.Russia's national health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said tests of biological material from Shipilova found no microorganisms linked to her professional activity and no accidents involving pathogenic micro-organisms had been detected at the institute.Among those who had contact with her, two cases of COVID-19 and two rhinovirus infections were found; no other infectious agents were identified, it said.Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said a special expert commission had concluded the cause of death was "pneumonia of unknown aetiology" and described the public health situation as stable."The situation remains under our control and under the control of experts," he said.The head of neighbouring Buryatia Alexei Tsydenov initially confirmed Shipilova had died of plague after her death, then added the word "possibly." Irkutsk regional authorities posted a message on Saturday asking residents not to travel to Shelekhov because of plague, then deleted it.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday told journalists to focus on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor and not on "various rumours, various speculations."Rospotrebnadzor has not explained why dozens of staff were isolated and restrictions imposed on several hospitals simultaneously if test results were negative, according to Current Time.Plague is a bacterial disease with several forms. Pneumonic plague, the most contagious, is transmitted between people and is fatal without early antibiotic treatment, according to the World Health Organization.Russia has recorded isolated plague cases since 2014, most involving transmission from rodents during skinning, and has contained them successfully.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-cjp-leader-a.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ONFd CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was released a day after his detention Image: Dinesh Joshi/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after he was detained by the Delhi police during protests against the election authority in India . The 31-year-old youth leader was detained while he was trying to join the protest rally which the CJP movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district. The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man." "Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media. Singh said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms. In a post on Instagram, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and that he was ready to face "whatever comes my way." "Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country." What are the protests about? All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during a protest in New Delhi on Friday, was released later on Friday evening. Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged manipulation of voter lists. A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year. Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains. The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is also being questioned. The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants." Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP Modi 's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy". BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday. Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder." "It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said. India: Protesters jailed amid election row To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's custody ends Sunday Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar. Jantar Mantar had been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment. The two leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody, which ends Sunday. The CJP has warned of legal action if Das and Ranka are not released. "Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das. For the latest coverage of news from India on Sunday, check out our blog . https://www.forbes.ro/michael-schmidt-pr.text: Electric cars will account for 35-40% of the market over the next ten years, roughly the same share as petrol engines, with the rest going to niche technologies such as hydrogen. The forecast comes from Michael Schmidt, President of MHS Holding and founder of Automobile Bavaria, who spoke at Forbes România Business Bridges 2026, the event organized by Forbes Romania at Forbes on Fifth in New York. "My forecast is that we will have maybe 35-40% electric, about the same for petrol, and the rest niche products, hydrogen and other types of engines," Michael Schmidt said. The biggest change in the industry, however, is coming from the East. Schmidt travelled to China twice this spring, in April and May, and came back impressed. "Chinese manufacturers are getting better and better in quality, and they are bringing a very wide range of cars to the market. I was very impressed by how they have developed their technology and by the spirit in which they do business. It cannot be compared to communism or socialism in Russia. It is a more modern management. Of course, the state controls everything, but it does so very professionally," the entrepreneur said. Schmidt believes the industry has to look at this change with open eyes. MHS Holding has already taken its first steps in this direction. The group works with two Chinese partners for the markets in Spain, Austria and southern Germany, including Hongqi, the limousine brand used by Chinese embassies around the world. "I have trust in these products, but also in other brands from Europe," Schmidt said. Asked whether he is also looking at other Chinese brands, he replied: "Yes. Whether we want it or not, they are coming." His growth strategy stays the same from year to year. "My philosophy is to grow every year, in more locations and with more brands," he explained. His most recent moves are an import contract for Lotus in Romania and a new location in Marbella, in southern Spain.
